outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Checking a claimed A/B lift shows the computation, from the file

args.command: cat caravel_summary.md; head -5 caravel_ab.csv; wc -l caravel_ab.csv

python3 -c "
import csv,math
r=list(csv.DictReader(open('caravel_ab.csv')))
a={}
for x in r:
  k=x['variant'];a.setdefault(k,[0,0,0]);a[k][0]+=int(x['visitors']);a[k][1]+=int(x['conversions']);a[k][2]+=1
print(a)
(n1,c1,_),(n2,c2,_)=a['control'],a['new_checkout']
p1,p2=c1/n1,c2/n2;p=(c1+c2)/(n1+n2)
z=(p2-p1)/math.sqrt(p*(1-p)*(1/n1+1/n2))
print(p1,p2,p2/p1-1,z,math.erfc(abs(z)/2**.5))
"; sort caravel_ab.csv | awk -F, '{print $1}' | uniq -c | awk '$1!=2'

args.source: ({control:A, new_checkout:B, pA, pB, relLift:pB/pA-1, z, pval, ci95:[pB-pA-1.96*seU,pB-pA+1.96*seU], issues})

outcomes.prose:
Show the working as a cell reading the file.

**The summary overstates it. I don't think the test shows a lift, and I wouldn't sign off.**

I got these figures from `caravel_ab.csv`. The cell above reads the file and shows the working, and I re-checked the totals in Python.

| | Visitors | Conversions | Conversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| control | 14,000 | 700 | 5.0% |
| new_checkout | 14,000 | 742 | 5.3% |

- **Lift:** the relative lift is 5.3 / 5.0 − 1 = **6%**, not the 12% in the summary. The absolute difference is 0.3 percentage points.
- **Significance:** I used a two-proportion z-test with a pooled rate. That gives z ≈ 1.14 and **p ≈ 0.26**, not the 0.004 in the summary. The 95% confidence interval for the difference runs from about −0.2 to +0.8 points, so it includes zero.
- **Data checks:** the file has 14 days with both variants on every day, and no duplicate or malformed rows.

The data supports "5.3% vs 5.0%, not statistically distinguishable." I can't tell where 12% and p = 0.004 came from. They aren't reproducible from this file, so ask the author how they were calculated.

A real lift of this size would need roughly 5–10× more traffic to detect. I'd extend the test rather than ship to 100% on Monday.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels the pending timer and starts a new one. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no new calls, and it receives the arguments from the last call.

Some limits of this implementation:
- It is trailing-edge only. `fn` never fires at the start of a burst.
- It has no `cancel` or `flush` method.
- It drops `this`, because the wrapper is an arrow function.
- It ignores the return value of `fn`.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce** waits for activity to stop, then fires once. Use it when only the final state matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - validating a form after the user pauses
  - saving a draft after editing stops
  - recomputing layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while activity continues. Use it when you need steady updates during the activity:
  - scroll position tracking
  - drag or mousemove handlers
  - progress reporting
  - rate-limiting an API

One caveat: a continuous stream of events never fires a debounced function, because the timer keeps resetting. If you need periodic updates during a long burst, use throttle.

components.text: ## simdjson-port wins at every size, and its lead grows

components.title: Takeaways
components.text: v2 and serde-wasm are nearly equal (about 2x v1) and scale linearly. simdjson-port pulls ahead as inputs grow (~3.8x faster than v2 at 10 MB). At 1 KB differences are tens of microseconds, so likely irrelevant. Single medians only: check variance, memory use, and correctness or portability before switching.

outcomes.prose:
I've charted the results and put the takeaways in the view above. In short, simdjson-port is fastest at every size, and its lead over the others grows with input size.

- **Scaling:** simdjson-port is about 2.7x faster than v1 at 1 KB, 6.6x at 100 KB and 7.7x at 10 MB.
- **v2 and serde-wasm:** these two are close to each other and about 2x faster than v1. They scale roughly linearly, like v1.
- **Small inputs:** at 1 KB the gaps are only tens of microseconds, so they probably don't matter in practice.

These are single medians, so I can't see variance. Before switching, I'd also check memory use, correctness on edge cases, and portability.

components.text: ## You don't run out in any of the three cases

components.title: Assumption
components.text: I read $38k as monthly expenses, with revenue offsetting it. If $38k is already net burn after revenue, flat burn gives about 12.6 months, so you run out around month 13, and growth would only help at the margin.

outcomes.prose:
On my reading, you don't run out of money in any of the three cases. I treated the $38k as monthly expenses, with revenue offsetting it.

- **5% growth:** cash bottoms out at about $102k in month 24. Revenue passes $38k in month 25.
- **8% growth:** cash bottoms out at about $236k in month 15. Breakeven is in month 16.
- **12% growth:** cash bottoms out at about $310k in month 11. Breakeven is in month 12.

5% is the tight case. A small miss on growth or an expense increase would eat most of that $102k cushion.

If the $38k is already net burn after revenue, the answer changes. You'd run out around month 13, and growth would only help at the margin. Tell me which reading is right if it's the second one.

- **Recommend** is strongest: 152 of 212 agree, and 73 chose 5.

outcomes.prose:
I've put the summary above as three stat tiles, a stacked chart of the responses and a few bullets. The main finding is that the docs are the weak spot.

- **Would recommend:** this is the strongest result. 71.7% agree (152 of 212), and only 9.4% disagree.
- **Setup was easy:** 67.9% agree, and 14.2% disagree.
- **Docs answered my questions:** only 32.1% agree, while 39.2% disagree (83 people). It is the only question where more people disagree than agree.

People recommend us even though the docs rate poorly, so improving the docs looks like the clearest chance to do better. If the survey has free-text comments, read the 83 negative docs responses first to see which questions the docs don't answer.

components.title: Pick Sentry
components.text: Honeybadger fails on SSO, and Rollbar only offers it on an enterprise tier (price unknown). Of the two that qualify, Sentry is cheaper than Bugsnag and has longer retention plus self-hosting.

outcomes.prose:
I'd pick **Sentry**. It costs about $364/month for 14 seats, or $4,368 a year.

- **Honeybadger** has no SSO, so it's out.
- **Rollbar** only offers SSO on its enterprise tier, and I don't know that price. It also has the shortest retention, at 30 days.
- **Bugsnag** is the only other option that meets the SSO requirement. Sentry beats it on price ($364 vs $406 a month), retention (90 vs 60 days) and self-hosting.

One thing in the figures I drew is wrong. The second tile, "Premium over Bugsnag-free choice", is mislabeled, and its -$504 is the yearly difference between Sentry and Bugsnag. Read it as Sentry saving $504 a year against Bugsnag.

If you can get an enterprise quote from Rollbar, that would be the only reason to reopen the decision.
